safety_layer2.search_summary:
Based on thorough research across multiple authoritative sources, here is a comprehensive answer regarding Forodesine's regulatory and safety history:

---

## Forodesine (Mundesine / Fodosine): Withdrawals, Black Box Warnings, and Discontinuations

### Summary Answer: **No market withdrawal for safety reasons, no FDA black box warning, but clinical development was discontinued in the US and Europe.**

---

### 1. 🚫 No FDA Black Box Warning


There is currently **no FDA Black Box Warning** for forodesine hydrochloride.


---

### 2. ❌ Not Withdrawn from Any Market for Safety Reasons

There is no record of forodesine appearing on any regulatory list of drugs withdrawn or removed from the market for safety or effectiveness reasons. The FDA's official list of such drugs (21 CFR § 216.24), maintained by the eCFR, does not include forodesine. (Source: [eCFR § 216.24](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-216/subpart-B/section-216.24))

Similarly, the Wikipedia [List of Withdrawn Drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_withdrawn_drugs) does not include forodesine.

---

### 3. ⚠️ Clinical Development Discontinued in the US and Europe (Not for Safety)


Although the **clinical development of forodesine was discontinued in the US and Europe**, a multicenter Phase I/II study of oral forodesine for relapsed peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL) was recently completed in Japan.
 The discontinuation in the US/Europe appears to have been driven by insufficient efficacy results in early trials rather than a formal safety-driven regulatory action.

---

### 4. ✅ Approved in Japan (2017) — Not Withdrawn


On 30th March 2017, the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare (MHLW) **approved MUNDESINE® (forodesine hydrochloride)** for the treatment of Relapsed or Refractory (R/R) Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma (PTCL).
 
The Ministry's decision followed successful clinical trials and made Japan the first country in the world to make Mundesine available for treatment of PTCL.
 There is no evidence that this approval has since been withdrawn.

---

### 5. 🔬 Still Investigational in the US and Europe


Forodesine's FDA approval status is currently **investigational** in the United States. It has received Orphan Drug designation for certain leukemias but is not yet approved for general public use in the US or Europe.


---

### 6. Known Side Effects (But Not Grounds for Withdrawal)


In general, the **toxicity of forodesine is manageable**.
 However, 
it is necessary to appropriately manage **opportunistic infections and secondary lymphomas** possibly associated with long-lasting lymphocytopenia caused by forodesine.
 Common side effects include 
gastrointestinal issues such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; fatigue, headache, and upper respiratory tract infections; and more severe but less common side effects including **neutropenia**.


---

### Sources:
- Liv Hospital Drug Profile: https://int.livhospital.com/drugs/forodesine-hydrochloride/
- Wikipedia – Forodesine: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forodesine
- Lymphoma Hub (MHLW Approval): https://lymphomahub.com/medical-information/mundesine-r-forodesine-hydrochloride-approved-by-japan-s-mhlw-for-relapsed-or-refractory-peripheral-t-cell-lymphoma
- BioCryst Press Release (GlobeNewswire): https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2017/04/03/953473/0/en/BioCryst-Announces-Mundipharma-Receives-Approval-for-Mundesine-in-Japan.html
- PMC/NIH Evidence-Based Review: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5916385/
- Synapse/PatSnap Drug Profile: https://synapse.patsnap.com/article/what-is-forodesine-hydrochloride-used-for
- eCFR § 216.24 (FDA Withdrawn Drug List): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-216/subpart-B/section-216.24
- DrugBank: https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB06185

---

**Bottom Line:** Forodesine has **never been withdrawn from a market for safety reasons**, has **no FDA black box warning**, and has **not been formally discontinued for safety reasons**. Its clinical development in the US and Europe stalled largely due to limited efficacy results. It remains approved and marketed in Japan as Mundesine for relapsed/refractory PTCL.

mechanism_direction.disease_mechanism_summary:
Here’s the target-focused assessment.

## 1) Disease mechanism

**Core defect:** *Hypermethioninemia encephalopathy due to adenosine kinase deficiency* is caused by **loss of function of ADK (adenosine kinase)**, not by abnormal PNP activity. ADK normally phosphorylates adenosine to AMP; when ADK is deficient, **adenosine accumulates**, which drives the **SAH hydrolase reaction toward S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) formation**, causing **elevated SAH and SAM, impaired transmethylation, and hypermethioninemia**. This is the primary molecular mechanism described in the original disease paper and subsequent reviews. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3188832/?utm_source=openai))

**What about PNP?** Based on the disease mechanism, **PNP is neither the primary deficient enzyme nor the overactive enzyme in this disorder**. The causal defect is **ADK deficiency**; the literature describing this disease does **not** identify PNP gain or loss as the primary molecular lesion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3188832/?utm_source=openai))

**Answer to Q1:**  
- Core pathophysiological defect: **ADK loss of function**, causing adenosine accumulation and disruption of the methionine cycle/transmethylation pathway. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3188832/?utm_source=openai))  
- **PNP in this disease:** **neither “deficient” nor “overactive” as the primary disease mechanism**; the relevant primary defect is upstream at **ADK**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3188832/?utm_source=openai))

## 2) Target-specific direction of forodesine on PNP

**Forodesine is a PNP inhibitor.** It was explicitly developed as a **purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) inhibitor**. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16131572/?utm_source=openai))

Since the disease defect in question is **not PNP overactivity**, inhibiting PNP does **not directly correct or compensate for the primary lesion**. In fact, focusing only on the drug’s direct action on **PNP itself**, **forodesine would push PNP activity downward**, i.e. toward a **PNP-deficient state**, which is **not the known defect in ADK deficiency**. Therefore, on a strict target-mechanism basis, **forodesine’s direct effect on PNP would not correct the disease defect and is better classified as potentially worsening/mismatching the defect rather than compensating for it**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3188832/?utm_source=openai))

A useful anchor is that **PNP deficiency itself is a recognized inborn error** with toxic deoxyguanosine/dGTP accumulation in immune cells; forodesine pharmacology intentionally mimics PNP deficiency to achieve T-cell toxicity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16131572/?utm_source=openai))

**Answer to Q2:**  
- **Would PNP inhibition correct the disease defect?** **No.**  
- **Direct action on PNP:** **does not compensate for ADK deficiency**; mechanistically it is more consistent with **worsening/misdirecting** the target state because it further suppresses PNP, a different enzyme. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3188832/?utm_source=openai))

## 3) Clinical use anchor

**Forodesine is not a known treatment for adenosine kinase deficiency.** The ADK-deficiency literature emphasizes supportive/metabolic management, including **methionine restriction**, not PNP inhibition. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8411109/?utm_source=openai))

**Forodesine is an approved/investigational PNP inhibitor for T-cell malignancies, not for PNP-defect disorders.** Clinical studies and regulatory documents describe it as a **PNP inhibitor** developed because **pharmacologic PNP inhibition can mimic aspects of inherited PNP deficiency**, leading to **deoxyguanosine accumulation, intracellular dGTP buildup, ribonucleotide reductase inhibition, and selective T-cell toxicity**. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16131572/?utm_source=openai))

For diseases caused by **PNP dysfunction itself**, the relevant dysfunction is typically **PNP deficiency**, an inborn error associated with immune dysfunction. A PNP inhibitor like forodesine would **not** be the confirmed therapeutic mechanism for such a disease; rather, it would be expected to **phenocopy** the deficiency state. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16131572/?utm_source=openai))

**Answer to Q3:**  
- **ADK deficiency / hypermethioninemia encephalopathy due to ADK deficiency:** No evidence found that forodesine is an approved, investigational, or validated treatment. Management in the literature centers on metabolic therapy such as methionine restriction. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8411109/?utm_source=openai))  
- **Disease caused by PNP dysfunction:** Forodesine is **not** a treatment for **PNP deficiency**; its confirmed clinical mechanism is the opposite context—**intentional PNP inhibition** to induce toxic dGTP accumulation in malignant T cells in **T-cell malignancies**. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16131572/?utm_source=openai))

## Bottom line

1. **Disease mechanism:** ADK deficiency is a **loss-of-function ADK disorder** causing adenosine accumulation and methionine-cycle disruption; **PNP is not the primary deficient or overactive target**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3188832/?utm_source=openai))  
2. **Direction on PNP:** Because forodesine **inhibits PNP**, its direct action on PNP would **not correct** ADK deficiency and is best viewed as **mechanistically mismatched / potentially worsening relative to the target direction**. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16131572/?utm_source=openai))  
3. **Clinical anchor:** Forodesine is used/investigated for **T-cell malignancies via PNP inhibition**, not for **ADK deficiency** or for treating **PNP deficiency disorders**. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16131572/?utm_source=openai))

Based on the search results from multiple authoritative sources, here is a comprehensive answer:

---

## Forodesine Hydrochloride: Safety Withdrawals, Black Box Warnings, and Discontinuations

**No.** Based on available evidence, **Forodesine Hydrochloride (brand name: Mundesine®)** has **not** been withdrawn from any market for safety reasons, received an FDA Black Box Warning, or been discontinued due to safety concerns. Here is a detailed breakdown:

---

### 1. 🚫 No FDA Black Box Warning


There is currently no FDA Black Box Warning for forodesine hydrochloride.


---

### 2. 🚫 No Market Withdrawal for Safety Reasons

A review of the FDA's official list of drugs withdrawn or removed from the market for safety or effectiveness reasons (21 CFR § 216.24, maintained at [eCFR](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-216/subpart-B/section-216.24)) does not include forodesine hydrochloride. Forodesine is not listed among the drugs on that roster.

---

### 3. 📋 Regulatory Status: Investigational in the US, Approved in Japan


Forodesine hydrochloride is currently investigational in the United States. It has received Orphan Drug designation for certain leukemias but is not yet approved for general public use in the US or Europe. It is approved for use in Japan for specific types of lymphoma.


Specifically, 
on 30th March 2017, the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare (MHLW) approved MUNDESINE® (forodesine hydrochloride) for the treatment of Relapsed or Refractory (R/R) Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma (PTCL).



The Ministry's decision followed successful clinical trials and made Japan the first country in the world to make Mundesine available for treatment of PTCL.


Since the drug has only ever been **formally approved in Japan**, and has not been approved (and thus cannot be "withdrawn") in the US or EU, there is no market from which it could be withdrawn for safety reasons in those jurisdictions.

---

### 4. ⚠️ Known Side Effects (But No Safety-Based Discontinuation)

While the drug has known adverse effects, these have not triggered regulatory safety actions such as a withdrawal or black box warning. Known side effects include:


Lymphopenia (a drop in white blood cells, which is expected because the drug targets these cells), opportunistic infections (because the drug lowers white blood cell counts, making the body less able to fight off viruses or fungi), and thrombocytopenia (a drop in platelets, which can lead to easy bruising or bleeding).


---

### 5. 🔬 Still Under Investigation


Forodesine hydrochloride is an investigational agent in many countries and is not currently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for general clinical use. It is available only through participation in approved clinical trials or in countries where it has received local regulatory approval.


---

Here is a comprehensive summary of what is known about **Pentostatin (brand name: Nipent)** regarding market withdrawal, black box warnings, and safety-related discontinuation:

---

## Pentostatin (Nipent): Safety Regulatory History

### ✅ Black Box Warning — YES

Pentostatin **does carry an FDA Black Box Warning** (the most serious type of warning the FDA can require). 
The drug must be administered under the supervision of an experienced cancer chemotherapy physician in a facility equipped to diagnose and manage complications, and recommended doses must not be exceeded.


The full scope of the Boxed Warning, as documented in the official FDA prescribing information, includes the following serious concerns:

- **Severe toxicity at higher doses:** 
Nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, central nervous system (CNS), and pulmonary toxicity occurred in Phase 1 studies that used higher doses than recommended.


- **Fatal pulmonary toxicity with fludarabine:** 
Pentostatin should not be used with concurrent fludarabine because of increased risk of pulmonary toxicity.
 This is confirmed in the official Pfizer prescribing information: 
The combined use of NIPENT and fludarabine phosphate is not recommended because it may be associated with an increased risk of fatal pulmonary toxicity.


- **Acute pulmonary edema and death in bone marrow transplant settings:** 
Acute pulmonary edema and hypotension, leading to death, have been reported in patients treated with pentostatin in combination with carmustine, etoposide and high dose cyclophosphamide as part of the ablative regimen for bone marrow transplant.


- **Nervous system toxicity:** 
Pentostatin treatment should be withheld or discontinued in patients showing evidence of nervous system toxicity.


- **Supervision requirement:** 
Pentostatin injection must be given under the supervision of a doctor who is experienced in giving chemotherapy medications for cancer.


📄 **Source:** FDA Prescribing Information (NIPENT™), 2025 label:
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/020122s021lbl.pdf
and Pfizer Medical Information: https://www.pfizermedical.com/nipent

---

### ❌ Market Withdrawal — NO

There is **no evidence** that pentostatin has ever been withdrawn from any market for safety reasons. 
Pentostatin received its initial FDA approval on October 11, 1991, for the treatment of adult patients with alpha-interferon-refractory hairy cell leukemia,
 and it remains an approved drug to this day.

📄 **Source:** HemOnc.org: https://hemonc.org/wiki/Pentostatin_(Nipent)

---

### ⚠️ Commercial Availability Concerns (Not a Safety Withdrawal)

While pentostatin has not been withdrawn for safety reasons, there are some commercial availability issues. 
Nipent is a brand name of pentostatin approved by the FDA, and while a generic version has also been approved by the FDA, FDA approval doesn't guarantee the generic will be available in pharmacies.
 
The generic medication may be approved, but does not appear to be commercially available at this time, and market launch delays can occur.
 This is a supply/commercial issue, **not** a safety-driven discontinuation.

📄 **Source:** Drugs.com Generic Nipent Availability: https://www.drugs.com/availability/generic-nipent.html

---

### ⚠️ Overdose / Higher Dose Safety Concerns


Administration of pentostatin in dosages higher than those currently recommended (20–50 mg/m² over 5 days as compared with 4 mg/m² every other week) has been associated with severe renal, hepatic, pulmonary, and CNS toxicity, which was unpredictable and occasionally fatal.


📄 **Source:** Healio Drug Information: https://www.healio.com/clinical-guidance/drugs/pentostatin

---

### Summary Table

| Category | Status |
|---|---|
| **Black Box Warning** | ✅ YES — Physician supervision required; no dose exceedance; fatal toxicity risks with fludarabine and certain combination regimens |
| **Market Withdrawal** | ❌ NO — Never withdrawn from any market for safety reasons |
| **Discontinued for Safety** | ❌ NO — Still FDA-approved and marketed as Nipent (Pfizer) |
| **Commercial Availability Issues** | ⚠️ Generic approved but may not be commercially available (not safety-related) |

Pentostatin remains a valid FDA-approved cancer treatment, but it is subject to serious warnings and must be used carefully within the recommended dosage parameters and under appropriate medical supervision.
